title: Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) Report - Ransomware Landscape in Africa 2024

1. executive_summary.content: In 2024, AFRINTEL documented 115 African victims publicly associated with ransomware, data-leak or access-sale activity (86 ransomware claims and 29 non-ransomware claims: 26 data-leak and 3 access-sale). The activity affected 27 countries, with a strong concentration in South Africa (30 victims, 26.1%), followed by Egypt, Algeria, Nigeria and Tunisia. The second half of the year was more active (70 victims, compared with 45 in the first half).
key_findings: LockBit3: most active ransomware group with 16 victims (18.6% of ransomware-attributed incidents)

2. methodology.content: This edition was fully recomputed from the 12 monthly AFRINTEL 2024 victim files (`CyberAttackAfrica/2024/*/victims.md`), the source of truth per project convention, which contain exactly 115 entries. It replaces a previous edition whose headline figure (90 entries) covered only a subset of the monthly records rather than the full annual dataset. Each entry is normalized by country, region, ransomware group or source actor where attributed, month of publication, sector and public domain. An incident is classified as Ransomware when a `Ransomware group` field is present and no explicit `Incident type` overrides it; Data Leak and Access Sale are used when the monthly card carries an explicit `Incident type` value. Sector statistics are grouped into macro-sectors using a documented keyword-based classifier to avoid misleading fragmentation. Country, sector and regional distributions cover all 115 entries; the ransomware-groups table covers only the 86 entries classified as Ransomware.
limitations: Data covering only public claims and public leak-site visibility.
Some victim descriptions remain limited when public business context is scarce.
Attribution based on the actor name associated with the public listing, not forensically confirmed.
Macro-sector groupings involve a degree of analytical judgment where a victim's activity spans multiple categories.

3. country_distribution.analytical_reading: South Africa alone represents more than a quarter of the 2024 dataset. This is consistent with its large digital economy, dense enterprise ecosystem, mature financial sector and high public visibility of ransomware claims.

4. industry_sector_distribution.analytical_reading: Financial services, insurance, banking and fintech-related entities form the most exposed macro-sector, reflecting the value of financial data and the pressure ransomware actors can apply. Government and public-sector bodies and the retail/e-commerce and technology/IT sectors are also highly represented, the latter creating a potential supply-chain risk.

5. ransomware_groups_activity.analytical_reading: LockBit3 remains the most visible ransomware actor in the AFRINTEL 2024 dataset, despite global disruption efforts. RansomHub and KillSec follow as major extortion actors with broad targeting. The long tail of smaller groups confirms the fragmentation of the ransomware/extortion ecosystem. Percentages in this section are computed against the 86 ransomware-attributed entries, not the overall 115-victim dataset.

6. geostrategic_regional_analysis.interpretation: Southern Africa is the main ransomware/exposure zone in 2024 (driven by South Africa, Namibia, Zimbabwe, Botswana and Zambia). North Africa follows, with Egypt and Algeria as the main drivers. Central Africa remains underrepresented in open-source ransomware visibility.

7. monthly_timeline_and_trends.trend_assessment: The second half of 2024 shows a clear increase in public ransomware/extortion visibility (70 victims versus 45 in the first half). This pattern suggests that African organizations should strengthen monitoring before holiday periods and month-end/quarter-end business cycles.

9. strategic_recommendations: Backup resilience: Apply the 3-2-1 rule, keep offline/immutable backups.
Identity security: Enforce MFA on VPN, RDP, cloud admin portals, email and privileged accounts.
Exposure management: Continuously audit exposed services and vulnerable applications.
Network segmentation: Separate critical servers, OT/ICS networks, backup infrastructure and admin workstations.
SOC correlation: Correlate authentication anomalies, endpoint discovery, archive creation and outbound data transfer.
Incident response: Maintain a ransomware playbook with legal, communications, technical and executive decision paths.
CTI monitoring: Track actor claims, but avoid overreliance on IoCs; prioritize TTP-based detection and sector exposure.
Ransom payment: Not recommended. It does not guarantee data recovery or non-disclosure and can fund further criminal activity.
sections.10. conclusion: The 2024 AFRINTEL dataset (115 documented records) confirms that ransomware and data-extortion actors are consistently targeting African organizations across public, private and critical sectors. The threat is not limited to a single region or industry. For 2025 and beyond, African SOC teams should prioritize identity hardening, exposed-service reduction, backup resilience, data-exfiltration detection and regional CTI sharing.
